hints: Start from what a base must do with its lone pair when it meets $\text{H}^{+}$, then compare how free that lone pair is in an amine versus an amide.
Look at the $\text{N}$ atom next to $\text{C=O}$ in an amide and think where its p-orbital lone pair can overlap and spread.
walkthrough:
Define what makes a nitrogen base strong**
Picture yourself as a proton, $\text{H}^{+}$, looking for electrons. A base is simply a species that can donate a lone pair to you to form a dative bond. In an amine, $\text{RNH}_{2}$, the lone pair sits localised on nitrogen, pointing outwards and fully available to grab $\text{H}^{+}$.

See why the amide lone pair is tied up**
Now look at an amide, $\text{RCONH}_{2}$. The nitrogen is directly attached to a strongly electron withdrawing $\text{C=O}$ group. The nitrogen p-orbital overlaps with the carbonyl pi system, so the lone pair is delocalised over N, C and O. Because that pair is already involved in this conjugation, it is far less available to coordinate to $\text{H}^{+}$, making amides essentially neutral and much weaker bases.

Final answer: A base acts by using a lone pair to accept / coordinate to $\text{H}^{+}$.
In amides the lone pair on N is delocalised into the $\text{C=O}$ group, so it is much less available to accept a proton than the localised lone pair in amines.

hints: Work backwards from 2-phenylethylamine, $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, and ask what functional group is reduced by $\text{H}_{2}/\text{Ni}$ to give a $\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$ group.
For the $\text{NH}_{3}$ route, recall which functional group undergoes nucleophilic substitution with excess ammonia to give a primary amine with the same carbon chain.
walkthrough:
Keep the carbon skeleton fixed**
The product is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. Both M and N must already contain the $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}$ unit. You are only changing the final functional group into $\text{NH}_{2}$.

Deduce M from catalytic hydrogenation**
$\text{H}_{2}/\text{Ni}$ reduces a nitrile, $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, to a primary amine: $$\text{R-CN} + 2\text{H}_{2} \xrightarrow{\text{Ni}} \text{R-CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$$ To get $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, R must be $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}$. So M is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$.

Deduce N from reaction with ammonia**
Excess $\text{NH}_{3}$ converts a halogenoalkane to a primary amine by nucleophilic substitution: $$\text{R-Br} + 2\text{NH}_{3} \rightarrow \text{R-NH}_{2} + \text{NH}_{4}\text{Br}$$ So N must be $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$, the bromoalkane with the identical skeleton.

Final answer: M is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CN}$ (phenylacetonitrile / 2-phenylethanenitrile).
N is $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$ (2-bromoethylbenzene, halogenoalkane with same $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}$ skeleton).

hints: Reaction 1 converts $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ to $\text{C}_{6}\text{H}_{5}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$, so identify the change at the $\text{C=O}$ carbon and recall the powerful hydride reagent needed for amides.
walkthrough:
Recognise a difficult carbonyl reduction**
Reaction 1 changes $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CONH}_{2}$ into $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{NH}_{2}$. The $\text{C=O}$ oxygen is removed as water and replaced by two hydrogens. Amides are very resistant to reduction, $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ or $\text{H}_{2}/\text{Ni}$ will not do it. You need the strongest common hydride donor, $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ in dry ether, which delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon and reduces the amide fully to the primary amine.
Final answer: $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ (lithium aluminium hydride, dry ether, followed by acid hydrolysis).

hints: Look at the $\text{C=O}$ on the left of H and count how many carbons are attached to that carbon, then count how many carbons are attached to the $\text{N-H}$ nitrogen.
walkthrough:
Classify both groups by counting attachments**
On the left, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH}_{2}$ has $\text{C=O}$ bonded to two other carbons, so it is a ketone, not an aldehyde. In the centre, the N is bonded to two carbon groups ($\text{CH}_{2}\text{C=O}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}$-cyclohexenyl) plus one H: $$\text{R}_{2}\text{NH}$$ That is the definition of a secondary, $2^{\circ}$, amine.

Final answer: other functional group: ketone (carbonyl).
classification of amine: secondary / $2^{\circ}$ amine.

hints: Treat ozone as a 1,3-dipole with a negative $\text{O}^{-}$ at one end and a positive $\text{O}^{+}$ in the middle, and decide which electron rich site of the alkene it first attacks.
Remember this step forms a five membered ring with three O atoms, so three pairs of electrons must move in a cycle: one from O, one from $\text{C=C}$, and one from $\text{O=O}$.
walkthrough:
Read the dipole**
The ozone shown as $^{-}\text{O}-\text{O}^{+}=\text{O}$ has a nucleophilic end ($\text{O}^{-}$ with a lone pair) and an electrophilic end (terminal $\text{O}$ of $\text{O}^{+}=\text{O}$). The alkene $\text{C=C}$ is electron rich. Ring formation needs concerted electron movement.

Push the three arrows in a loop**
Start arrow 1 at the $\text{O}^{-}$ lone pair pointing to one C of the $\text{C=C}$ to make a new C-O bond. As that C gains a bond, the $\text{C=C}$ pi pair must leave, so arrow 2 goes from the $\text{C=C}$ bond to the terminal O of the $\text{O=O}$ to make the second C-O bond. That O would then have too many bonds, so arrow 3 goes from the $\text{O=O}$ pi bond onto the central $\text{O}^{+}$ to neutralise the charges. The result is the five membered C-C-O-O-O ozonide ring.

Final answer: Curly arrow 1: from lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to C of $\text{C=C}$.
Curly arrow 2: from $\text{C=C}$ pi bond to terminal O of $\text{O=O}$.
Curly arrow 3: from $\text{O=O}$ pi bond to $\text{O}^{+}$ (forming the cyclic ozonide).

hints: L is a single molecule with two $\text{C=O}$ groups formed by cutting one $\text{C=C}$, so ask whether K must be open chain or cyclic and join the two carbonyl carbons back together with a double bond.
walkthrough:
Reverse the cleavage**
Ozonolysis cuts each $\text{C=C}$ into two $\text{C=O}$ groups. Here one alkene K, $\text{C}_{8}\text{H}_{14}$, gives one product L containing both carbonyls: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(=O)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{C(=O)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$. That can only happen if K was cyclic, the double bond being inside the ring. Mentally remove the two O atoms and join the two carbonyl carbons with $\text{C=C}$. The three $\text{CH}_{2}$ groups between them plus the two $\text{C=C}$ carbons make a five membered ring. The left carbonyl carbon carried $\text{CH}_{3}$ and the right carried $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, so K is a cyclopentene with methyl and ethyl substituents on the double bond.

Final answer: K is 1-methyl-2-ethylcyclopent-1-ene: a five membered ring with $\text{C=C}$ bearing $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ groups (cyclisation of L by joining the two $\text{C=O}$ carbons).
